name: Audio-Visual Systems
title: Audio-Visual Systems
answer: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art treat sound and image as one responsive medium, not two separate tracks. They appear in installations, live performance, projection mapping, and immersive rooms where the audience's presence or movement changes what is seen and heard. The work often sits between composition, animation, and interface design, and it may use sensors, cameras, microphones, or networked devices to close the loop. The site's index of 2000 audio models and 1000 video models gives a sense of how many components a practitioner can draw on, though most projects use only a few.

sections.body: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art treat sound and image as one responsive medium, not two separate tracks. They appear in installations, live performance, projection mapping, and immersive rooms where the audience's presence or movement changes what is seen and heard. The work often sits between composition, animation, and interface design, and it may use sensors, cameras, microphones, or networked devices to close the loop. The site's index of 2000 audio models and 1000 video models gives a sense of how many components a practitioner can draw on, though most projects use only a few.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for these systems is typically a computer with a GPU, audio interface, and a set of libraries for real-time signal processing and graphics. Practitioners often use environments like Max, TouchDesigner, Pure Data, or openFrameworks, which handle audio and video together and allow custom control logic. For machine learning components, they may call pre-trained models for source separation, style transfer, or gesture recognition, sometimes on the same machine and sometimes over a network. Latency, synchronization, and clock drift are constant concerns because sound and image must stay aligned to within a few milliseconds for the illusion to hold.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The process usually starts with a concept for an experience, then moves to prototyping the sensing and mapping between input and output. Artists build a patch or a script that takes data from microphones, cameras, or motion sensors and translates it into parameters for sound synthesis and visual rendering. They iterate in the studio, then adapt to the venue, because room acoustics, lighting, and audience flow change the piece. Machine learning may enter as a trained model for classification or generation, but it is often one module among many, and the artist tunes its behavior through rehearsal and testing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Audio-visual systems raise questions about who owns the output when a model is trained on existing music, film, or images. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, a reminder that the legal ground is unsettled. Provenance matters for datasets and for the models themselves, and artists may need to document their sources and licenses. There are also physical risks in installation work, such as hearing damage from high sound levels, eye strain from projection, and trip hazards from cables, so safety planning is part of the practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward tighter integration of generative models with real-time systems, so that sound and image can be synthesized together rather than separately. Smaller, faster models on edge devices may allow more responsive installations without a heavy server. At the same time, the growth of AI music services and the lawsuits around them will shape what artists can use and how they credit it. The site's 686 glossary terms suggest that the vocabulary is still expanding, and practitioners will need to keep track of both technical and legal shifts.
